title: This Ancient Fish Brain Holds Secrets to How Animals First Walked
summary:
How did animals first learn to walk on land? A fish fossil from Antarctica is giving scientists new clues. The fish, called Koharalepis jarviki, lived about 380 million years ago during the Devonian Period—a time known as the "Age of Fishes" because the oceans were full of all kinds of fish. 

Researchers used a special kind of scanner, like a super-powered X-ray, to peek inside the fish's skull without breaking it. They found that its brain was a lot like the brains of fish that were starting to move onto land. That's a big deal because Koharalepis is related to the very first four-legged animals, called tetrapods. 

The scans also showed that this fish had openings on top of its head for breathing air, and a special organ in its brain that could sense light and help it keep track of day and night. These features probably helped it live in shallow water, where it could gulp air from the surface. 

Koharalepis was about the size of a baseball bat—around 1 meter long—and it was a sneaky hunter. It had small eyes, so it likely used other senses to catch smaller animals. This fossil is the only one of its kind ever found, making it extra precious. By studying it, scientists are piecing together the amazing story of how fish eventually left the water and became land animals.
why_it_matters: This fossil shows how life on Earth changed over millions of years, and studying it helps us understand our own deep history as animals with backbones.

background_read: The Devonian Period, about 419 to 359 million years ago, is often called the ‘Age of Fishes’ because many strange fish species lived then.
Some fish from that time developed lungs and strong fins, allowing them to crawl onto land; these became the first tetrapods (four-legged creatures).
Fossils from Antarctica show that the continent was once much warmer and connected to other landmasses before they drifted apart.
Article_Structure: WHO: Scientists studying a rare fossil fish named Koharalepis jarviki.
WHAT: The fish fossil revealed brain features linking it to the first land animals.
WHERE: Found in Antarctica; the fish lived in shallow water.
WHY: To understand how fish started walking on land and evolved into tetrapods.

perspectives.description: Scientists are excited because this rare fossil fills in gaps about the evolution of land animals.
Some might say studying a single fossil isn’t enough to prove how all animals evolved, but it’s a vital piece of the puzzle.
The careful use of advanced scanners shows how technology helps paleontology without damaging precious fossils.
